name: Lime
lede: Lime is the yellowish green of the lime fruit, and the same word names the white caustic mineral that coated walls, set fresco and sat in dye vats for thousands of years.

sections.title: A fruit and a mineral
sections.body:
Lime is two words that look alike. As a color it is the green or yellowish green of the lime fruit [1]. St Clair adds that the shade has drifted from the fruit and is now usually much more luminous, even neon [2]. As a material it is something else entirely: calcium oxide, the white caustic powder made by burning limestone, which painters, plasterers and dyers used for thousands of years [3][4].

The two meanings meet in the color words. Paterson lists lime for the fruit color, lime white for the color of calcium oxide, and lime green for a pale or greenish-yellow green, with lime yellow and lime blue beside them [1]. Our library dates lime green as a color name in English to about 1883, an approximate date from the name's first appearances [13]. The books do not say who used the word first.

sections.title: Lime the mineral
sections.body:
Strictly speaking, lime is calcium oxide, made by heating limestone to about 900 degrees Celsius until the calcium carbonate gives up its carbon dioxide [3]. Add water and it slakes into calcium hydroxide, the putty used in mortar and the limewash painted on walls [3]. As the paint dries it takes carbon dioxide back from the air and turns again into calcium carbonate, a slow process that can take years to finish [3]. The Latin word for lime, *calx*, is the root of calcium, calcite and calcination [3].

That is why lime white is the oldest of wall colors. In fresco the plaster is made of sand and lime, and the pigments are brushed onto it while it is still wet, so that the lime binds the sand and slowly turns to chalky calcium carbonate over the color [5]. Paterson defines lime-resisting colors as those that do not react to alkali and so can be applied to fresh plaster [1]. Cennino Cennini, Ball notes, describes a sky blue made by mixing Baghdad indigo with white lead or with lime white [6].

Lime white has a plain virtue and a plain fault. Finlay reports that chalks and limes did not alter with time, and unlike lead white they were safe to use with orpiment, but they look thin and transparent in oil [7]. The cheaper lime whites also had to be repainted every year [7].

sections.title: Whitewash and plague
sections.body: Lime was also public health. Finlay says that in early twentieth-century Hong Kong, whitening walls with lime was thought the best precaution against plague, and police raided slum houses that were not white enough [7]. St Clair dates a whitewashing campaign to the 1894 Hong Kong plague and describes whitewash as a cheap paint of lime and salt that flakes off yearly and acts as a disinfectant [8]. The two books disagree on the date, so the campaign can only be placed between 1894 and the early 1900s [7][8].

sections.title: Lime in the dye vat
sections.body: Dyers needed lime too, and not for its color. Balfour-Paul describes how the indigo leaf is steeped in water until it ferments, then drained, and slaked lime is stirred in so that oxygen can precipitate the indigo as a blue paste; in Sumatra and Thailand the lime comes from burnt shells [9]. A Japanese indigo dyer will add rice bran, rice wine, honey or lime to speed the fermentation in the vat [10]. An English woad vat recipe quoted by Garfield calls for a quarter of a peck of dry slaked lime among other things [11]. Ball adds that medieval lye, the strong alkali used to draw dyes out of plants, was made from soda and quicklime [5].

sections.title: Lime blue, lime green
sections.body: The color trade also used lime as a prefix. Lime blue is a copper pigment related to blue verditer, thought to take its name from the lime used in making it, and the Pigment Compendium records one author's recipe that mixes it with gypsum [4]. Lime green, in Bersch's 1901 account, is a mixture of copper arsenite and calcium sulfate, listed in the Colour Index as CI 77412 and treated as a synonym for patent green [4]. Lime-arsenic green is a less common name for [[emerald]] green, which was likewise an arsenic pigment [4]. In nineteenth-century paint catalogues, then, lime green could mean a poisonous pigment, not a fruit.

sections.title: Limelight
sections.body: Lime also lit the stage. Paterson notes that stage lighting before electricity was made by burning lime, and the word limelight records that [1]. Gage places the lime-light at about 1820 and says Charles Babbage, a scientist, planned a ballet in the 1840s with four colored lime-lights, red, yellow, blue and purple, drifting and overlapping across dancers dressed in white [12].

sections.title: Lime on cloth and shell
sections.body:
Lime green is a color that fades into other colors. Finlay describes Tipu Sultan's war coat, captured in 1799, as hot pink and lime green with orange pompoms; by 1972 its silks had faded mostly to brown [13]. In Oaxaca, Finlay watched a sea snail's milky secretion rubbed onto white thread: it made a fluorescent lime-green stain that within a few minutes turned yellow and then purple in the sunlight [14]. The snail is *Purpura pansa*, and its dye is a cousin of the ancient shellfish purple, [[tyrian-purple]], with the green as its first stage in light [14].

Our modern lime is a later invention. St Clair notes that fluorescent colors became fashionable in the 1970s, that Crayola issued a box of eight fluorescent crayons in 1972, and that the X-Ray Spex single "The Day the World Turned Day-Glo" came out in 1978 with a lime background on its cover [2][15]. True fluorescent dyes absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as visible light, which is why highlighter inks glow [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
Our Lime is #BFFF00, a vivid yellowish green [13]. It is not the lime of the web. In CSS and the X11 color set, lime is #00FF00, pure green, and LimeGreen is a darker #32CD32 [1][13]. The fruit sits nearer our swatch, which the ISCC-NBS system would call a brilliant yellow green, about 8.6 units away [13].

Colors are not fixed by their surroundings, either. Eckstut shows a turquoise circle and a lime circle that are in fact the same color, made to look different only by the colors around them [16]. Its closest relatives in our color list are [[lime-green]], [[lime-yellow]], [[chartreuse]] and [[green-yellow]] [13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering even one per cent of its canvas, within four CIEDE2000 units, as photographed [17]. That describes this archive, not painting as a whole, and a color this saturated is rare in aged, varnished canvases [17]. The lime that painters did use was the white of the wall [5]. In printed English the adjective lime, as in lime green, peaks in the 1920s [18].
